title: SiteGuard's statistics function becomes a route to root
overview: Attackers are exploiting SiteGuard's web application firewall to run commands as root or SYSTEM, and remediation can erase attack traces. A KVM escape puts private-cloud hosts at risk, while ConnectWise expands its Microsoft 365 incident figures. Three critical plugin flaws also need attention.
paragraphs: Good morning, it's 5:22 AM. Monday, the nineteenth of October, twenty twenty-six.

The firewall meant to keep attacks away from your web server is letting attackers run commands on it instead. SiteGuard Server Edition, a Japanese web application firewall, has an OS command injection flaw in its statistics function. That function is enabled by default. Both the vendor and Japan's CERT agency say exploitation is confirmed, and the commands run as root or SYSTEM. Not merely access to a website: control of the machine underneath it.

The flaw is CVE-2026-106931, affecting versions from 2 point 20 onwards, before 8 point 00 Update 5, or before 7 point 00 Update 6 on FreeBSD. Exploitation needs statistics processing active. SiteGuard claims to protect more than one and a half million websites, though that isn't a count of vulnerable installations. Neither advisory tells us who's been hit or how widely the attacks have spread.

There's a particularly awkward catch with fixing it: remediation may erase attack traces. Before changing anything, save the “Diagnostic information” from the web management screen. I'd make that part of the change ticket, not a note somebody finds afterwards. Then install 8 point 00 Update 5, or 7 point 00 Update 6 on FreeBSD. If an upgrade isn't possible, the vendor also offers replacement statistics-processing files, including for end-of-life versions. That's a useful escape hatch for an old server that can't move today.

And a boundary failing underneath the workload is the problem with PwnEscape, too. Here it's a malicious guest reaching into a Linux KVM host, rather than an attacker getting through a web firewall. KVM is the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel; on affected x86 systems, a few malformed IPv4 packets can expose host memory and potentially lead to code execution on the host.

The clever bit is the timing. The packet header has already passed validation when guest-controlled checksum metadata influences where a checksum gets written. Repeat the disclosure and the guest can collect host memory. Paulos Yibelo at Pwn.ai found it using AI vulnerability research tools, and the kernel team has patched it as CVE-2026-99999. There's no known exploitation.

AWS says EC2 isn't at risk, but private clouds and KVM-based products such as Proxmox and Nutanix are exposed. Take the fixed Debian or RHEL kernels as they arrive; Ubuntu hosts need their distribution's update too. Plan the hypervisor reboots, moving guests where needed, and treat untrusted guest workloads as hostile until then. I'd put the reboot window on the calendar now. A kernel package waiting on disk isn't the finish line.

From the host boundary to the tenant boundary: there's more detail on yesterday's ConnectWise incident. Huntress now counts three hundred tenants with successful sign-ins, out of almost a thousand targeted. A second wave against sixteen tenants failed. ConnectWise says it identified the issue on the fourteenth of October, and revoked certificates at seven AM UTC on Saturday the seventeenth.

It also says seven application identities have been disabled, covering Cloud Backup and Cloud Management integrations. The named integrations include MS Teams and Exchange Online, alongside MS Graph. Partner Center and SharePoint Online are named too. SaaS Security and Cloud Management are now offline out of caution as well. That widens the service disruption beyond the backup outage we discussed yesterday, and gives administrators more specific application names to match against their tenant inventories.

Back on web-facing software, two unauthenticated plugin flaws score nine point eight: privilege escalation in Brainstorm Force OttoKit through 1 point 1 point 40, and object injection in QuantumCloud Conversational Forms for ChatBot through 1 point 5 point 1. Arraytics Booktics through 1 point 0 point 29 has unauthenticated SQL injection at nine point three; check the vendors for fixed releases and update all three.

I'd give an exposed SiteGuard installation the first change window, with its diagnostic export safely saved beforehand. For KVM estates, keep an eye on distribution kernel releases so the host reboot doesn't drift into next week's problem. Have a good Monday.
